title: India Transforming into a Global Healthcare Powerhouse Through Indigenous Research, Innovation and Affordable Advanced Treatment; Dr. Jitendra Singh Calls for Judicious Balance Between Clinical Medicine and Technology-Driven Practices
subtitle:
Dr. Jitendra Singh says India's growing scientific capabilities, genomic diversity and indigenous medical breakthroughs are opening new frontiers in global healthcare
Indian Genome Programme, indigenous antibiotics, HPV vaccination, gene therapy and CAR-T cell treatment reflect country's growing strength in advanced medical research
Minister releases official souvenir of Global Healthcare Conclave 2026; interacts with young medical students and encourages them to embrace emerging technologies
AI, precision medicine and preventive healthcare to play a defining role in India's healthcare journey towards Viksit Bharat 2047
body_text: Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, today said that India is undergoing a significant transformation in healthcare, moving towards becoming a global powerhouse through indigenous research, medical innovation and affordable advanced treatment. Emphasising the importance of maintaining a judicious balance between clinical medicine and technology driven practices and clinical judgement, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that while AI, quantum technologies and advanced diagnostic tools are transforming healthcare, technology cannot replace the fundamental clinical understanding required of a doctor. He said that medical education must continue to place strong emphasis on bedside learning, direct patient interaction, clinical examination and practical experience. Dr Jitendra Singh said that the country, which once depended considerably on foreign medical technologies and advanced treatment facilities, is now developing indigenous solutions in vaccines, antibiotics, gene therapy and cancer treatment, while emerging as a cost-effective destination for quality healthcare. The Minister said that India's growing scientific capabilities, unique genomic diversity and advancements in precision medicine have created unprecedented opportunities to contribute to global healthcare, adding that the next generation of doctors must combine technological advancements with strong clinical acumen to address the evolving challenges of modern medicine. Dr. Jitendra Singh was addressing the Global Healthcare Conclave 2026, organised by the Global Association of Indian Medical Students (GAIMS). The conclave brought together young medical students, healthcare professionals and members of the medical fraternity to deliberate on emerging developments, opportunities and challenges in healthcare. Dr. Minu Bhajpai, Vice President, National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), attended as the Guest of Honour, while Dr. Shubham Anand, National Chairman, GAIMS, and other members of the organisation's executive were present. The Minister released the official souvenir of the Global Healthcare Conclave 2026 and also interacted with young medical students. Recalling the transformation of India's healthcare ecosystem over the past several decades, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that medical science has progressed from conventional X-ray-based diagnostics to advanced technologies such as ultrasound, CT scans and MRI, alongside significant advancements in therapeutics and disease management. He said that while communicable diseases once accounted for a major share of morbidity and mortality, India is now facing a dual burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases, with Type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, dyslipidemia and fatty liver disease emerging as major public health challenges. The Minister said that India's extraordinary genetic and population diversity provides a unique resource for medical research, with the country's diverse population groups offering valuable opportunities to understand genetic variations and disease patterns. Referring to the Indian Genome Programme, he said that around 10,000-15,000 individuals from 84 different populations have already been sequenced, with an initial target of reaching one million individuals. This extensive genomic database has the potential to strengthen India's precision medicine capabilities and generate scientific knowledge that could benefit healthcare research across the world. Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the convergence of genomics, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies is creating new possibilities for personalised and targeted treatment. Referring to ongoing scientific initiatives, he mentioned research aimed at genetically engineering E. coli to produce GLP analogues, which could help address insulin resistance and associated metabolic conditions. He said that such research reflects the growing focus on developing scientific solutions to India's specific healthcare challenges. The Minister also referred to the changing disease profile of the country, particularly the increasing incidence of metabolic disorders among younger populations. He said that Type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular conditions and fatty liver disease are increasingly being detected at younger ages, making it essential to strengthen research into the relationship between metabolic disorders and develop more targeted approaches to prevention and treatment. Dr. Jitendra Singh said that India has made significant progress in establishing itself as a global centre for healthcare innovation, moving beyond its earlier role as primarily a manufacturing destination for medical products developed elsewhere. He referred to India's achievements in vaccine development and the country's growing contribution to global vaccination efforts. He also mentioned the HPV vaccination programme, under which more than 50 lakh adolescent girls have already been vaccinated. The Minister said that India has also made important advances in indigenous antibiotic development, with two indigenously developed antibiotics emerging in the last two years, one of which is being marketed by Wockhardt. He said that these developments reflect the country's increasing capacity to undertake research, develop new molecules and create solutions for diseases that were earlier addressed largely through imported technologies and products. Referring to advanced medical research, Dr. Jitendra Singh cited successful gene therapy trial work for haemophilia at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore, published in the New England Journal of Medicine. He said that the achievement demonstrates India's growing ability to contribute to cutting-edge medical research and develop solutions for complex diseases. The Minister also referred to CAR-T cell therapy and the cancer research at Tata Memorial Centre, Mumbai, as an important example of India's progress in making advanced cancer treatment more cost-effective. The Minister said that such indigenous innovations are strengthening India's position in advanced healthcare and creating opportunities for Indian medical professionals and researchers to contribute at the global level. Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the global perception of Indian medical professionals has also changed significantly, with Indian doctors and researchers gaining increasing recognition for their capabilities, knowledge and contribution to medical science. He said that the country's achievements in vaccines, antibiotics, advanced cancer therapies and medical research have enhanced India's stature internationally, giving young Indian doctors a stronger platform to participate in global healthcare. Drawing from his own experience as a medical practitioner, the Minister recalled how earlier generations of doctors developed clinical expertise through extensive hospital exposure and direct interaction with patients. He said that the ability to identify symptoms, assess clinical conditions and arrive at a diagnosis through observation and experience remains fundamental to medical practice. He expressed concern over excessive dependence on diagnostic investigations, stressing that investigations must be interpreted in the context of clinical findings rather than becoming a substitute for clinical assessment. Dr. Jitendra Singh encouraged medical students to remain curious learners and continuously update their knowledge in emerging areas such as Artificial Intelligence, quantum technologies, genomics and precision medicine. He said that these technologies offer fascinating possibilities, including more targeted treatments and improved diagnostic capabilities, but doctors must exercise sound judgement in their application. The Minister also suggested that the medical education system should give greater consideration to clinical competence and practical exposure in postgraduate medical training and selection. He said that the development of clinical sense requires sustained patient interaction and hands-on experience, and that a doctor should be capable of providing medical assistance even in situations where advanced equipment and diagnostic facilities are unavailable. Highlighting the government's efforts to strengthen access to affordable healthcare, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that initiatives such as Ayushman Bharat have expanded financial protection for patients, including provisions covering pre-existing diseases. He also referred to the expansion of dialysis facilities across district hospitals as an important step towards improving access to essential healthcare services. The Minister said that prevention will be one of the defining features of healthcare in the coming years, particularly as lifestyle-related and metabolic disorders are increasingly affecting younger people. He referred to the distinctive pattern of central obesity among Indian populations, explaining that individuals who may appear physically lean can also have significant visceral fat, which is an independent risk factor for metabolic and cardiovascular conditions. He stressed the importance of generating India-specific medical data to better understand such disease patterns and develop appropriate interventions. He said that healthcare organisations such as GAIMS have an important opportunity to contribute beyond conventional medical education by actively participating in research, healthcare delivery, public health advocacy and collaboration with the private sector. He encouraged young medical professionals to utilise the expanding opportunities in India's scientific and healthcare ecosystem and contribute towards addressing the country's emerging health challenges. Dr. Jitendra Singh said that India is at a particularly promising stage in its healthcare journey, with indigenous research, technological advancements, a growing scientific ecosystem and globally recognised medical professionals creating new opportunities. He expressed confidence that young doctors, through their contribution to research, innovation and patient care, would play a significant role in strengthening India's healthcare capabilities and advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. ***** SG/AK
